Q: Numpy array converts to truncated string when saving Pandas df to Dask A:

This isn’t coming from dd.from_pandas() or compute(). It happens because you’re round-tripping through CSV with an object column that contains numpy.ndarray values.

  • A pandas column can only have a real dtype for a limited set of types (ints/floats/datetimes/strings/categoricals, etc.).
  • If you store a np.ndarray in a cell, the column becomes dtype=object -> i.e. "a bunch of arbitrary Python objects".

And you are saving it to csv. CSV is just text. It can’t store "an ndarray in a cell", doesn't store any metadata needed to reconstruct such objects. So when pandas/dask writes that object column it has to convert each cell to a string. For ndarrays that means:

str(arr)  # which calls np.array2string(arr)

And NumPy’s str() for long arrays is abbreviated by default, so you get .... That ... is not just display: it’s literally what gets written to the CSV, so after reading it back you only have the string and the middle values are gone.

Fixes:

  1. Don’t use CSV for this (easiest solution): store as Parquet. Parquet keeps types/metadata and is the default "native" format for Dask.
  2. Normalize it (often the best design). If your tooling allows it, don’t keep "array per row". Store samples in a separate table like a relational DB:
main table: id, metadata…

samples table: id (FK), idx, value

This is usually more efficient for storage and queries (filtering, aggregations, joins), and it works great with Parquet too.

  1. If you must stick to one table and need compact storage, use an explicit encoding. Maybe store bytes (arr.tobytes()) instead of relying on str(ndarray).

Q: How should I be using Dask .compute() to perform relatively simple operations A:

Some of your CSVs are probably just missing the "date" column!

When your call .compute(), Dask reads the CSVs and discovers the missing column, raising KeyError, while if you only use a subset of the partitions, you get lucky and your subset has the named columns

If you're sure it's only the headers which are bad, you can probably do any number of fixes (though cleaning up data before passing it to Dask is generally ideal, it's not always possible to get clean data)

While it's not as efficient as a more advanced reader (actually it's a lot worse as this will read twice and use twice the disk space..), consider using the workers to fix the data headers rather than having complex parsing every time .. however, if you have enough memory or don't want to re-save the files double, you can fix the files in-memory with a custom reader function .. as long as it returns a Pandas DataFrame right away, you can use .from_map() to pull all the data together in a more custom way, allowing you to inspect every or the first few lines or whatever else you need!

from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path  # just for easier globbing

from dask.distributed import Client
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

def read_csv_wrapper(path):
    with open(path) as fh, StringIO() as buffer:
        for lineno, line in enumerate(fh):  # NOTE each line will end with "\n"!
            if line.startswith("foo"):  # ignore foolines!
                continue
            # opportunity for more cleanup, such as your headers
            # opportunity to verify the contents
            buffer.write(line)
        buffer.seek(0)  # rewind file pointer to the beginning for reading
        return pd.read_csv(buffer)

...
client = Client(...)
ddf = dd.from_map(read_csv_wrapper, Path("tmp/").glob("*.csv"))

Finally, if you have some other weird format or worse malforming of your CSVs, Matt Rocklin (the original author of Dask) provides some insight into how to do a completely custom reader from a bytes format Reading custom file format to Dask dataframe

Q: What's the best way to handle a callback (wiith named type) that might be unsafe if misused? A:

I am leaning towards this option now.

My opinion changed partly based on this comment, and partly based on realising that it would be sound for such a type to implement Consumer if all its constructors were unsafe – that way, the constructors could specify a safety condition that the newly constructed callback were only used with the correct sort of argument. The documentation of my type would then be enough to allow the user to determine that the safety condition of the consumer's constructor would be satisfied.

Q: How can I control the shutdown order of Spring-managed beans that I don’t create myself? A:

Do you have graceful shutdown enabled? (see docs for Boot 4.0)

This might worth an issue for Spring Boot to change the shutdown behavior and shut down the registry after the webserver stops receiving traffic.

Q: List all remote branches that are behind master A:

Since git 2.13.0 added --no-contains you can just do:

git branch --remote --no-contains master

This will show all remote branches that do not contain the commit that master currently points at in their history -- i.e. the ones that are "behind" master.

Q: Unexpected hex value for float A:

This is due to issues relating to the difference between 32-bit and 64-bit. You should check your compiler settings, as it is currently being treated as a 64-bit double. Floats are often automatically converted to doubles.
